narr: In this section, we'll explore the history of Uzbekistan during the Soviet period and its path to independence.
Let's begin by examining the cultural policies and demographic changes during this era.

data.heading: Cultural Policies
bullets: Language policy: compulsory Russian study in 1938
Introduction of Cyrillic script in 1940
Russian raised to state language status

narr: The Soviet regime implemented several cultural policies aimed at Russification.
First, in 1938, the study of Russian became compulsory in national schools, with reduced hours for native languages.
Then, in 1940, the Cyrillic script was officially introduced by decree.
Finally, Russian was elevated to the status of a state language, further diminishing the prominence of local languages.

data.heading: Migrations and Centralization
bullets: Policy of artificial increase of multinational composition
Forced and voluntary resettlement
First deported groups: Koreans, Germans, Poles

narr: The Soviet Union pursued a policy of artificially increasing the multinational composition of republics.
This involved both forced and uncontrolled voluntary resettlement of various ethnic groups.
Among the first to be deported were the Koreans of the Far East, the Germans of the Volga region, and the Poles of western Ukraine and Belorussia.
Between September and December 1937 alone, more than 74,500 Koreans arrived in Uzbekistan.

data.heading: Additional Deportations
bullets: 1943-1944: Political exiles from North Caucasus, Georgia, and Crimea
Approximately 110,000 Meskhetian Turks from Georgia
151,424 Crimean Tatars from Crimea

narr: During 1943-1944, Uzbekistan received additional waves of deportees.
These included political exiles from the North Caucasus, Georgia, and Crimea.
Specifically, about 110,000 Meskhetian Turks were deported from Georgia.
And 151,424 Crimean Tatars were forcibly relocated from Crimea to Uzbekistan.

data.heading: Central Control
bullets: Uzbekistan remained strictly subordinate to the central government
Article 17(c): Even establishment of borders required approval
Regional divisions also subject to Supreme Soviet approval

narr: Throughout this period, Uzbekistan remained strictly subordinate to the central Soviet authorities.
Under Article 17(c) of the Soviet constitution, even the establishment of borders within Uzbekistan required approval.
Similarly, the division of regions into districts was subject to approval by the Supreme Soviet of the USSR.
This centralized control limited local autonomy and decision-making power.

data.heading: Contribution to Victory in WWII
bullets: 1,433,230 people participated - over 40% of able-bodied population
263,005 killed, 132,670 missing in action
395,795 did not return, 60,452 became invalids

narr: Uzbekistan made a significant contribution to the victory over fascism in World War II.
A total of 1,433,230 people from Uzbekistan participated in the war, representing more than 40% of the republic's able-bodied population.
The human cost was tremendous: 263,005 were killed, 132,670 went missing in action.
Additionally, 395,795 did not return from the war, and 60,452 became invalids due to their service.

data.heading: Military Honors
bullets: About 120,000 soldiers awarded orders and medals
280 received the title of Hero of the Soviet Union
75 of the Heroes were Uzbeks

narr: Despite the heavy losses, Uzbek soldiers received significant recognition for their bravery.
About 120,000 soldiers from Uzbekistan were awarded various orders and medals for their service.
A total of 280 individuals from Uzbekistan received the prestigious title of Hero of the Soviet Union.
Among these heroes, 75 were Uzbeks, highlighting the ethnic diversity of those recognized.

data.heading: Industrial Evacuation
bullets: Industry put on war footing
More than 100 enterprises evacuated from Russia, Ukraine, Belorussia
Over 1 million evacuees received, including 200,000 children

narr: During the war, Uzbekistan's industry was put on a war footing to support the Soviet war effort.
More than 100 industrial enterprises were evacuated and relocated to Uzbekistan from Russia, Ukraine, and Belorussia.
The republic also received over 1 million evacuees from occupied districts, including 200,000 children.
To accommodate these children, orphanages were opened, and many were adopted by Uzbek families.

data.heading: Cultural Contributions During War
bullets: Publication of works on Alisher Navoi
Works of classics: Lutfi, Bedil
Poems: 'Shirin and Shakar', 'Kunduz and Yolduz', 'Dalli', 'Muradkhan', 'Malika ayor'

narr: Despite the hardships of war, Uzbekistan continued to make cultural contributions.
During the war years, two volumes on the life and work of Alisher Navoi were published.
Works of classical Uzbek literature by authors like Lutfi and Bedil were also distributed.
Notable poems published included 'Shirin and Shakar', 'Kunduz and Yolduz', 'Dalli', 'Muradkhan', and 'Malika ayor'.

data.heading: Post-Stalin Era
bullets: De-Stalinization and rehabilitation of victims
National policy changed little despite de-Stalinization
Sharaf Rashidov's important role (1960s-early 1980s)

narr: After Stalin's death, the Soviet Union entered a period of de-Stalinization.
This included the rehabilitation of victims of political genocide, though the general approach to national policy changed little.
Sharaf Rashidov played an important role during this period, serving as the First Secretary of the Communist Party of Uzbekistan from the 1960s to the early 1980s.
Under his leadership, dozens of large industrial enterprises were opened in Uzbekistan.

data.heading: Industrial Development
bullets: By 1985: 1,549 enterprises functioning
Sectors: machine-building, chemistry, construction, light industry, agro-industrial
Irrigation: 197,000 km of canals, 23 reservoirs with 10 billion cubic meters capacity

narr: During Rashidov's leadership, Uzbekistan experienced significant industrial development.
By 1985, 1,549 enterprises were operating in sectors including machine-building, chemistry, construction, light industry, and agro-industrial branches.
The republic also expanded its irrigation infrastructure, developing 197,000 kilometers of canals.
Additionally, 23 reservoirs were constructed with a total capacity of 10 billion cubic meters of water.

data.heading: Economic Losses
bullets: Specialization as raw material supplier
1980s: 250+ billion cubic meters of gas annually
50+ tonnes of gold annually
Cobalt, molybdenum, tungsten, copper, uranium exports

narr: Despite industrial growth, Uzbekistan suffered significant economic losses during this period.
The republic was specialized as a raw material supplier to the Soviet center.
In the 1980s alone, annual deliveries of gas exceeded 250 billion cubic meters, and gold production exceeded 50 tonnes.
Uzbekistan also continuously exported cobalt, molybdenum, tungsten, refined copper, and uranium to other Soviet regions.

data.heading: Resource Extraction
bullets: Minerals worth ~$5.5 billion annually
Gold and rare metals revenues didn't reach Uzbek treasury
Last 15 years of USSR: '$35 billion cotton and gold' taken
Total mineral value delivered to center: over $75 billion

narr: The value of minerals extracted from Uzbekistan was substantial.
Annually, minerals worth approximately $5.5 billion were extracted from the republic.
Crucially, the revenues from the sale of gold and rare metals did not reach the treasury of Uzbekistan.
In the last 15 years of the USSR, resources worth no less than $35 billion in 'cotton and gold' were taken for the needs of the central government.
The total value of all minerals delivered to central regions exceeded $75 billion during this period.

data.heading: Environmental Consequences
bullets: Cotton monoculture
Uncontrolled use of Amu Darya and Syr Darya waters
Tragedy of the Aral Sea

narr: The Soviet economic policies had severe environmental consequences for Uzbekistan.
The focus on cotton monoculture led to intensive water usage for irrigation.
The uncontrolled use of the waters of the Amu Darya and Syr Darya rivers disrupted the regional ecosystem.
These practices ultimately led to the ecological disaster known as the tragedy of the Aral Sea, which dramatically shrank due to reduced water inflow.

data.heading: Perestroika and Independence Movement
bullets: M. Gorbachev's 'Perestroika' (April 1985)
'New thinking' in foreign policy
National movements for democratic reform and sovereignty
1989: Demonstrations in Fergana, Kokand, Kuvasay, Gulistan, Parkent, Buka

narr: In April 1985, Mikhail Gorbachev proclaimed 'Perestroika,' offering hope to exit the systemic crisis.
This policy introduced 'new thinking' in foreign policy, emphasizing 'universal human values' and 'a world without violence and war'.
These reforms sparked national movements across Uzbekistan with demands for democratic reform and genuine sovereignty.
In 1989, a wave of demonstrations swept through cities including Fergana, Kokand, Kuvasay, Gulistan, Parkent, and Buka.

data.heading: Islam Karimov's Rise
bullets: Elected president in March 1990 ( unprecedented step)
First union region to elect a president
Center's negative reaction
Emphasis on political sovereignty and economic self-reliance

narr: In March 1990, Islam Karimov was elected president of the Uzbek SSR, an unprecedented step.
No other union region had previously elected a president, making this a significant development.
The central Soviet government reacted extremely negatively to this move.
Karimov advanced the idea of political sovereignty and economic self-reliance as decisive conditions for independence.

data.heading: National Reforms
bullets: 1989: Uzbek language given state language status
Measures to eliminate cotton monoculture
Efforts to restore spirituality
August 1989: Resolution on personal subsidiary plots
Early 1990: Employment programme
July 1990: Decree on water supply and rural gasification

narr: During this period, several national reforms were implemented.
In 1989, the Uzbek language was given the status of the state language.
Measures were taken to liquidate the cotton monoculture and to restore cultural and spiritual heritage.
In August 1989, a resolution was passed on personal subsidiary plots to support private agriculture.
At the beginning of 1990, an employment programme was introduced.
And in July 1990, a decree was issued to improve water supply and gasify the countryside.

data.heading: Declaration of Independence
bullets: Adopted June 18-20, 1990
12 articles enshrining key principles
Supremacy of democratic state and laws
Independent resolution of internal and foreign policy questions
Respect for international law principles

narr: On June 18-20, 1990, the Supreme Soviet of Uzbekistan adopted the Declaration of Independence.
This document consisted of 12 articles that enshrined key principles for the republic's future.
It established the supremacy of the democratic state and its laws throughout the territory.
The declaration affirmed the right to independently resolve internal and foreign-policy questions.
It also emphasized recognition of and respect for the basic principles of international law.

data.heading: Path to Formal Independence
bullets: August 19, 1991: Failed coup attempt (GKChP)
Emergency session adopted Statement on independence
August 31, 1991: Independence proclaimed
September 1 declared Independence Day

narr: On August 19, 1991, the last attempt to preserve the USSR occurred with an unconstitutional coup d'état.
The coup, led by the State Committee for the State of Emergency (GKChP), isolated Gorbachev.
In response, an emergency session of the Supreme Soviet adopted the Statement on the independence of Uzbekistan.
On August 31, 1991, independence was officially proclaimed.
By resolution, September 1 was declared Independence Day and a national holiday beginning in 1991.

data.heading: Sovereign State Establishment
bullets: Referendum on independence (people's support test)
First nationwide presidential elections
Constitutional Law 'On the Foundations of State Independence'
Adoption of state symbols (emblem, flag, anthem)
Introduction of national currency (sum)

narr: Following the declaration, steps were taken to establish Uzbekistan as a fully sovereign state.
A referendum was held to test the people's support for independence.
The first nationwide presidential elections were conducted.
A Constitutional Law 'On the Foundations of State Independence' was enacted.
State symbols including the emblem, flag, and anthem were adopted.
Finally, the national currency, the sum, was introduced as a basic attribute of sovereignty.
Now, let's examine some key questions from the textbook with their model answers.
These questions help understand the fundamental concepts of Uzbekistan's history during this period.

data.heading: Question 1
data.problem: What was the main idea behind the creation of new republics in the Soviet Union?

steps.text: The idea of nation-building through the creation of national republics on the linguistic principle
Goal to build 'homo sovieticus' - a person who thinks, behaves and lives in the Soviet way
Separation of peoples living in one locality by languages
Imposition of moderate 'Soviet' values with preference for non-Muslim traditions
Republics created without sovereignty under ideological homogenization of the CPSU

data.result: The creation of new republics was based on the idea of nation-building to establish 'homo sovieticus' through linguistic separation and imposition of Soviet values, without genuine sovereignty.

narr: Let's consider our first question about the creation of new republics in the Soviet Union.
The model answer explains that this was based on the idea of nation-building.
The Soviet Union created national republics on the linguistic principle to build 'homo sovieticus'.
This involved separating peoples living in the same locality by languages.
Instead of centuries-old traditions, moderate 'Soviet' values were imposed, with preference for non-Muslim traditions.
Importantly, these republics were created without genuine sovereignty, under the ideological control of the Communist Party.

data.heading: Question 2
data.problem: Why did the Soviet Union pursue a harsh repressive policy?

steps.text: Repression as an instrument for building 'homo sovieticus'
Physical reprisal against the intelligentsia and influential people
Maintaining loyalty through fear and control

data.result: Repression was used to build 'homo sovieticus' and suppress resistance through physical reprisals against intellectuals and intimidation to maintain loyalty.

narr: Our second question asks why the Soviet Union pursued such a harsh repressive policy.
The answer explains that repression served as a key instrument for building 'homo sovieticus'.
Physical reprisals against the intelligentsia and influential people helped facilitate the spread of Soviet ideology.
This process was described as 'watering' Soviet ideology through intimidation.
Ultimately, these repressive measures were designed to maintain loyalty and control over the population.
